## Goal

Fit and inspect a response calibration, invert it with its concentration basis
intact, distinguish range from independent QC and residual review, and interpret
a conditional inverse uncertainty interval. Use the chemistry and design to
justify the report before exporting a number.

## Background

For a linear response $y=a+bc+e$, set known concentration c and measure y.
An unknown point estimate is $(\bar y-a)/b$, not a reversed regression. Retain
the intercept unless a justified measurement model specifies otherwise. A good
$R^2$ cannot rule out curvature, matrix effects, drift or preparation loss.

The supplied iron calibration uses mg elemental Fe/L in a final coloured solution
and absorbance already referenced to a reagent blank. A method blank, independent
check and sample spike answer different questions. All data are simulated.

## By hand

**B1.** A line is $y=0.010+0.200c$, with c in mg/L final. A mean unknown response
0.510 follows a fivefold preparation dilution. Calculate final and original
concentration. [Hint](#hint-b1)

**B2.** Someone forces that line through zero while keeping slope 0.200. What
estimate results from response 0.510? Why is concentration zero not sufficient
reason to force a measured response through zero? [Hint](#hint-b2)

**B3.** At c=2 mg/L, the line in B1 predicts 0.410. An observation is 0.440.
Calculate the residual and explain its sign. Would one residual identify an
instrumental cause? [Hint](#hint-b3)

**B4.** An independently sourced 2.00 mg/L check is estimated as 1.70 mg/L.
The preselected exercise window is 95–105% recovery. Calculate recovery and the
action for affected unknowns. [Hint](#hint-b4)

**B5.** In a separate ideal low-level model, blank SD is 0.004 signal units and
sensitivity 0.500 signal units per mg/L. Calculate the rough 3-SD concentration
increment. Is it a universally validated detection limit or proof of zero below
that value? [Hint](#hint-b5)

## Explore {#explore}

The demo uses a monotonic toy response
$y=0.010+0.200c/(1+qc)$ plus independent response noise, with q in L/mg.
q=0 is linear; positive q gives a saturating curve. Standards, later sample and
independent check are separate records. The known truth is visible only because
this is a simulation; it does not appear in real unknown data.

**E1.** Set q=0 and response noise to zero. Why is a sample result withheld while
residual review is pending? Accept the line after inspecting it, and check the
5 mg/L original unknown at dilution factor 2. [Hint](#hint-explore)

**E2.** Set largest standard to 8 mg/L and q to 0.015 L/mg, retaining zero noise.
Compare $R^2$ with residual structure. What would rejecting the line mean, and
what evidence would a narrower proposed range still need? [Hint](#hint-explore)

**E3.** Reset to a linear response, largest standard 4 mg/L and accepted review.
Set original unknown to 20 mg/L and dilution factor 1. Then make a new simulated
measurement at factor 10. Explain why this is different from editing the
preparation factor on the old response. [Hint](#hint-explore)

**E4.** With an in-range sample, change later sensitivity by −20%. Which check
sees this failure? Can the old standards' residuals diagnose later drift?
[Hint](#hint-explore)

## In R

Run from the supplied project root. These are the reviewed iron data, separate
from the toy saturating-response demo. They cover 0–4 mg Fe/L in final solution.

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
standards <- read_csv("data/standards.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit <- lm(absorbance ~ standard_mg_l, data = standards)
a <- unname(coef(fit)[1])
b <- unname(coef(fit)[2])
standards <- standards |>
  mutate(fitted = fitted(fit), residual = residuals(fit))
ggplot(standards, aes(standard_mg_l, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Final iron concentration (mg Fe/L)", y = "Residual absorbance") +
  theme_minimal()
unknown <- c(.47922, .48041, .48223)
limits <- predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(standard_mg_l = c(0, 4)))
in_range <- all(unknown >= limits[1] & unknown <= limits[2])
candidate_final <- if (in_range) (mean(unknown) - a) / b else NA_real_
candidate_final
source("R/inverse-calibration.R")
conditional_interval <- inverse_calibration(fit, unknown)
conditional_interval
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(conditional_interval, "output/calibration-unknown.csv")
```

**R1.** Interpret a and b with units, inspect the residuals, and state the final
concentration estimate. Why is it not yet an original-water result?
[Hint](#hint-r1)

**R2.** Interpret the helper's standard uncertainty and approximate 95% interval.
Name its assumptions and at least two omitted sources. Explain why a forward
response interval is not itself a concentration interval. [Hint](#hint-r2)

**R3.** Fit the deliberately curved dataset and plot its residuals. Explain what
a model/range review would need, without deleting inconvenient standards merely
to improve the graph. [Hint](#hint-r3)

```r
curved <- read_csv("data/course/nonlinear-calibration.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
curved_fit <- lm(response ~ c_mg_l, data = curved)
curved <- curved |> mutate(residual = residuals(curved_fit))
ggplot(curved, aes(c_mg_l, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Concentration (mg/L)", y = "Residual response") + theme_minimal()
```

**R4.** Export `calibration-range-and-qc.csv` and save it at the project root.
Fit **only standard rows**, not unknown or check rows. Match the demo's
coefficients and explain why the independent QC is not another point to include
in the fit. [Hint](#hint-r4)

```r
if (file.exists("calibration-range-and-qc.csv")) {
  demo <- read_csv("calibration-range-and-qc.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
  demo_standards <- demo |> filter(role == "standard")
  demo_fit <- lm(response ~ known_final_mg_l, data = demo_standards)
  print(coef(demo_fit))
  print(demo |> filter(role == "independent_check"))
}
```

## Hints

::: {#hint-b1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B1"}
Subtract the fitted intercept before dividing by slope. Then reverse the
preparation dilution to return to the original basis.
:::

::: {#hint-b2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B2"}
Compare $0.510/0.200$ with $(0.510-0.010)/0.200$. A response can have a background
offset even at nominal concentration zero.
:::

::: {#hint-b3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B3"}
Residual is observed minus fitted. The sign locates a point relative to a line;
it does not identify a chemical or instrumental mechanism by itself.
:::

::: {#hint-b4 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B4"}
Recovery is $100\times c_{estimated}/c_{reference}$. Apply the preselected rule
before deciding on a reportable result.
:::

::: {#hint-b5 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B5"}
Use $3s/b$. A complete detection procedure also needs its noise, blank, matrix
and decision-probability conditions.
:::

::: {#hint-explore .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hints E1–E4"}
Range, independent QC and residual review are separate requirements. A simulator
can expose the generating truth, but a real unknown cannot be validated merely
by looking at a hidden correct answer.
:::

::: {#hint-r1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R1"}
[`lm()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/lm.html)
fits absorbance as response. Prepared concentration is the explanatory variable.
Volume/preparation records connect final solution to original sample.
:::

::: {#hint-r2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R2"}
The helper propagates reading noise and the fitted intercept/slope covariance
through an inverse relation. It excludes preparation and recovery effects.
:::

::: {#hint-r3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R3"}
[`residuals()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/residuals.html)
can show curvature despite a high overall association. A justified range needs
adequate standards and checks for the intended sample responses.
:::

::: {#hint-r4 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R4"}
Including the check in calibration sacrifices its independent role. Filter by
`role`, not by row position or whichever rows make the result look best.
:::

## Solutions

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions B1–B5"}
**B1.** $(0.510-0.010)/0.200=2.50$ mg/L final; original concentration is
$2.50\times5=12.5$ mg/L. Both units and material stage belong in the report.

**B2.** A forced-zero calculation gives 2.55 mg/L final, 2% above 2.50 mg/L.
A nominal zero concentration does not guarantee a precisely zero response. The
intercept must follow the justified model and evidence, not convenience.

**B3.** $0.440-0.410=+0.030$ signal units. The point lies above the fitted line.
One residual alone does not establish its cause; a pattern across concentration
may support investigation of model failure.

**B4.** Recovery is $100(1.70/2.00)=85.0\%$, failing the supplied 95–105% rule.
Withhold affected unknowns, investigate, restore satisfactory calibration/checks
and remeasure as appropriate. Dividing all results by 0.85 would assume a cause
not established by the failed check.

**B5.** $3(0.004)/0.500=0.024$ mg/L is a rough blank-relative concentration
increment. It is not universal validation, and a below-limit response is not
proof of exactly zero analyte.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions E1–E4"}
**E1.** A model review has not yet been made, so a numerical candidate is not
automatically reportable. With q=0, noise=0, accepted review and satisfactory
range/QC, a=0.010 and b=0.200 give 2.50 mg/L final and 5.00 mg/L original.

**E2.** Positive q gives diminishing sensitivity and systematic residual
structure despite high $R^2$. Rejecting the line withholds the simple estimate.
A narrower range may reduce nonlinearity, but needs adequate standards,
diagnostics, independent checks and suitable intended sample responses; it is
not validated by removing inconvenient points.

**E3.** At factor 1 the final concentration is 20 mg/L, beyond the four mg/L
calibration. A new factor-10 measurement gives 2 mg/L final and returns to
20 mg/L original. It supplies a new observed response; changing a number beside
the old out-of-range response supplies no new measurement.

**E4.** Under the linear zero-noise model a −20% sensitivity change gives an
independent-check recovery of 80%, so affected samples are withheld. The old
calibration residuals still look perfect because they predate the change.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions R1–R4"}
**R1.** a≈0.003873883 absorbance units; b≈0.198799368 L/mg Fe. Final estimate
is 2.3981269 mg Fe/L. The residuals lack obvious curvature in this selected range,
though that does not prove sample recovery or selectivity. Original-water
concentration also needs the actual aliquot and final-volume factor.

**R2.** The supplied helper gives standard uncertainty about 0.0045090 mg Fe/L
and approximate 95% interval 2.388568–2.407686 mg Fe/L **final**. It assumes a
correct linear model, independent normal equal-variance response errors,
negligible calibration-concentration uncertainty and a well-determined positive
slope. Sampling, volume uncertainty, matrix bias and recovery are omitted. A
forward interval has response units; inverse concentration limits require the
uncertain inverse relation, including intercept/slope covariance. The helper
uses a first-order approximation, not a general nonlinear inverse algorithm.

**R3.** Curved-response residuals show a systematic concentration pattern. This
is evidence against the single straight-line model over that full range, not
permission to erase standards until $R^2$ looks satisfactory. A proposed range
or model needs independent evidence and fit to the analytical purpose.

**R4.** `filter(role == "standard")` reproduces the fitted coefficients within
numerical rounding. The check material tests whether the selected calibration
predicts an independently known quantity; fitting it into the same line would
reduce its ability to reveal failure. Unknown rows do not supply known
calibration concentrations in an actual analysis.
:::

## Where this leads

[UV/visible absorption](../uv-visible/exercise.qmd) supplies the absorbing species,
measurement path and preparation chemistry behind the iron response. All later
methods revisit range, independent checks and honest uncertainty statements.
